#45762. Meet Linde Freya Tangelder, Nendo's pick for the most influential designer of the next 20 years

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1514 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dezeen ↗ Open Full Page

Meet Linde Freya Tangelder, Nendo's pick for the most influential designer of the next 20 years

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1514 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nendo has selected Linde Freya Tangelder for Dezeen’s 20×20 project in partnership with Kohler.
  • Insofar as she creates furniture and lighting, Tangelder is technically a designer, but only just.
  • According to recent reports, “How I think is not typical design,” she told Dezeen.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nendo has selected Linde Freya Tangelder for Dezeen’s 20×20 project in partnership with Kohler. In this interview, the Dutch designer explains why she doesn’t find design inspiring.

Insofar as she creates furniture and lighting, Tangelder is technically a designer, but only just.

According to recent reports, “How I think is not typical design,” she told Dezeen. “So I’m never thinking about function in the first place. The whole process is very intuitive, it’s just a cloud of connections in my head – more about concepts or stories that I want to tell rather than making a functional piece.”.

“I’ve never been so inspired by design in general,” she added. “It’s a skill that fits very well to me, but I’d rather connect it in inspiration to art, to architecture, or another discipline.”.

With a highly sculptural style, Tangelder also sometimes refers to herself as an artist – a label she claims she wouldn’t have dared use when starting out.

She has made a name for herself through pieces that often play with unexpected juxtapositions of materials and use traditional methods of production to create an unmistakably contemporary aesthetic.

Recent findings suggest that “I like to use poor materials, rich materials, and fuse them,” she explained. “For me, it’s sort of a synonym for how I think culture should be.”.

In 2019, she was identified by Dezeen as a young designer to watch after exhibiting at Collectible, as well as winning that year’s Biennale Interieur designer of the year award.

Explaining the studio’s decision to select her as a 20×20 nomination, Nendo praised Tangelder’s approach for being “both remarkably gentle and quietly bold”.

“Driven by a playful curiosity to take architecture apart and put it back together, she reveals qualities in familiar materials that we have long overlooked,” the studio told Dezeen.

Referencing buildings in the medium of furniture has become something of a calling card for Tangelder.

Notable examples include the Bolder Chair, which recalls architectural columns, the Windows of Bo Bardi table, which mimics the shape of windows on the SESC Pompéia Factory in São Paulo, and Brick’s Reflection Chair with its terracotta backrest (pictured left).

These propensities are reflected evocatively in the name of Tangelder’s studio – Destroyers/Builders – though recently, she tends to work more under her own name.

“I’m inspired by architecture, things I see in buildings,” she stated. “I think it’s just really interesting to scale it down to the field of artistic design, or limited-edition design.”.

According to recent reports, “In the history of architecture there’s so much to tell,” she continued. “For me it’s more diverse and also less superficial than the history of design, and I think that’s what interests me so much.”.

“And also that it feels more essential, I think that is maybe the core. I just like brick. I like simple materials that are used for construction rather than smooth finishes just for decoration.”.

Not that she is completely opposed to smooth, decorative finishes – as evidenced by the fact that an entire room in the home-slash-studio that she shares with her landscape-architect partner is used exclusively for lacquering.

In fact, most of the house, which is in a leafy area outside Brussels, is taken up by Tangelder’s atelier space.

She moved to Belgium shortly after graduating from Design Academy Eindhoven in 2013, and has become part of an increasingly rich design scene in the country over the past decade.

It has been revealed that in the first years it was quite a struggle to start from out of nothing. Just to survive and make it happen, and to earn a project back – there’s so much investment in each project.

“I moved to Belgium because I really like the culture, the art scene, architecture as well,” said Tangelder. “The design scene I thought was actually quite minimal, or I didn’t really see a lot of studios at that time. But I liked that as well, it felt a little bit more new for me.”.

Sources indicate that “I think it developed a lot, the landscape in design in Belgium over the last 10 years,” she considered. “There’s a lot happening right now.”.

It has certainly been a productive decade for Tangelder, whose back-catalogue is impressively extensive considering she has only ever employed a very small number of assistants.

Part of that has been made possible thanks to collaborations with the healthy network of craftspeople across Belgium that Tangelder has established to help with production.

According to recent reports, “That has been super important for me,” she said. “Each material that I really love, I have a partner now.”.

But moreover, the chunky portfolio is a reflection of a huge amount of hours spent working in the studio. Though she claims her work-life balance is improving, Tangelder works almost every day including weekends, and has been known to go years without a holiday.

“I really like it, so for me it’s the best way to spend my time,” she stated, before pausing.

“I should think about it more as fun time, because of course it’s also a struggle. You’re always struggling over all the decisions that have to be made.”.

Recent findings suggest that so that means you take risks all the time. It’s maybe more intense, but also more fun.

Like many independent designers, Tangelder has had to battle to earn a living from her discipline.

“In the first years it was quite a struggle to start from out of nothing,” she remembered. “Just to survive and make it happen, and to earn a project back – there’s so much investment in each project.”.

Over time, she says she has acquired a reasonably good sense of which pieces are likely to prove more lucrative, though she has resisted the temptation to focus her energies entirely on these.

“I think when you decide to only continue projects that you know will have commercial success, then it will be less experimental,” she explained.

“So that means you take risks all the time,” she added. “It’s maybe more intense, but also more fun.”.

Most of Tangelder’s work involves one-off or limited-edition pieces for galleries, but she has also partnered with brands.

A major moment came in 2022 when she was commissioned by Cassina to produce a collection of side tables and pouffes, and she has continued to work with the Italian brand each year since.

This year she was able to put on a solo exhibition at Milan design week supported by Cassina, showcasing a combination of her independent pieces and products created for the brand.

I just think the material is very me. That desk light tells a lot about how I like to see objects. It’s really in between a sculpture and a functional object.

It was an unusual example of small-scale making and larger-scale production design being displayed side-by-side.

Far from being a barrier to creative expression, Tangelder has found that these commissions can be an enabler by providing up-front revenues, unlike solo work.

“So it gives less pressure, I would say, which is very good for the creative process,” she noted.

But you can have too much of a good thing, and while she enjoys the more collaborative experience of working for a brand she limits this type of work to two projects per year to ensure she has plenty of time for her own pieces.

Sources indicate that tangelder’s current obsession is cast and oxidised metal, so she reports spending a lot of time these days in a foundry in Antwerp. Her most recent piece is a grungy take on a conventional desk lamp, in white bronze.

In a recent development, “I just think the material is very me,” she remarked. “That desk light tells a lot about how I like to see objects. It’s really in between a sculpture and a functional object.”.

Looking to the future, she is interested in working more with fashion, having previously designed a chair for Dior.

And, she would like to work on a larger-scale installation – perhaps an outdoor sculpture, she suggests.

In a world where for various reasons the boundary between design and art is increasingly blurred, Tangelder is undoubtedly at the forefront.

She is an interesting 20/20 choice from Sato, who is typically associated with minimalist, highly functional product design.

For her part, Tangelder sees her work as partly an indirect response to the Sato approach – a continuation of a conversation.

“I have, of course, quite a different form language, but I think it’s also a reaction to what he’s done,” she mentioned.

“He’s so clear in the decisions that he makes, he’s a master in it, and I’m really grateful that he sees what I’ve been doing.”.

Picture this: you're standing at the gate for your Boston weekend trip, and the person next to you just swiped their credit card for $280 to book the exact same seat you're sitting in — a seat that cost you 7,500 Avios and maybe $5.60 in taxes. That's the British Airways Avios short-haul sweet spot in action, and once you see it, you can never unsee it. This is the redemption the ChooseFI community quietly uses to stretch their points further than almost any other domestic award. While everyone else is chasing first-class international awards (which are spectacular, don't get us wrong), this sweet spot lets you turn a modest points balance into a steady stream of nearly free regional flights — year-round, on American Airlines metal, with zero fuel surcharges. Here's the math that makes it click: A last-minute nonstop flight from Fresh York (JFK/LGA) to Boston Logan or Los Angeles (LAX) to San Francisco typically runs anywhere from $150 to $300 in cash. You're paying that for roughly a one-hour flight — the kind of trip where by the time the flight attendant hands you a drink, you're already starting your descent. British Airways prices that same flight at a flat **7,500 Avios**. At a $200 cash fare, that's **2.67 cents per point (CPP)** — well above the standard valuation most programs offer for domestic economy. At a $300 last-minute fare, you're looking at **4 cents per point**, which is exceptional for any award program, let alone a simple domestic booking. The pricing inefficiency is hiding in plain sight: British Airways uses a **distance-based award chart**, which means short flights cost proportionally fewer points. The U.S. domestic short-haul zone (under 650 miles) sits at 7,500 Avios one-way — a price that hasn't ballooned with inflation the way cash fares have. Every time airfare spikes for a holiday weekend or a last-minute booking, your Avios redemption looks better and better. For the FI-minded traveler, this redemption is pure arbitrage: you're converting transferable points that cost you perhaps 1–1.5 cents each to earn into travel worth 2–4 cents each in real-world value. That's a 2–4x return, consistently, on routes you'd likely be flying anyway.

The magic here lives inside British Airways' distance-based award chart — and understanding why it's structured this way is the 'aha moment' that turns a confusing loyalty program into a tool you actually want to use.

Most U.S. airline programs (Delta, United, American) have largely abandoned distance-based pricing in favor of dynamic or zone-based awards that tend to price popular routes higher. British Airways never fully made that switch for partner awards. Their Avios chart still prices flights primarily by the number of miles flown between origin and destination. A flight under 650 miles costs 7,500 Avios one-way in economy — full stop. It doesn't matter if it's a Tuesday in February or the Sunday after Thanksgiving. The chart price holds.

The Partner Piece: Why You're Booking AA, Not BA.

According to recent reports, here's the critical nuance that trips up new people: British Airways charges notoriously high fuel surcharges on its own operated flights. We're talking $300–800+ in carrier-imposed fees on top of the Avios. That would completely wipe out the value of this redemption. But when you book American Airlines-operated flights through British Airways Avios, those surcharges disappear entirely. AA does not pass fuel surcharges to partner award bookings. Your out-of-pocket cost is typically just the government taxes — often $5–15 each way.

This is the non-negotiable rule: always book AA metal through British Airways Avios, not BA-operated flights.

British Airways allows open-jaw routing on Avios awards. Industry News: What Is ‘Nonnamaxxing’? The Italian Grandma Lifestyle Might Be the Secret to Longevity

📅 10 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1512 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that when I moved to Italy in 2024, one of the first things I noticed was the very particular way Italian nonne, or grandmas, live.
  • Industry observers note that I was then delighted—and unsurprised—when I came across a newly introduced wellness trend making the rounds on social media.
  • Sources indicate that there’s certainly a lot to learn from Italian grandmothers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that when I moved to Italy in 2024, one of the first things I noticed was the very particular way Italian nonne, or grandmas, live. They walk everywhere, frequently across the city, without any assistance. Many of them are dressed to the nines, but they also don’t try to hide their age.

Industry observers note that I was then delighted—and unsurprised—when I came across a newly introduced wellness trend making the rounds on social media. “Nonnamaxxing” is the idea that anyone can maximize their life if they just embrace the habits of Italian grandmas. It happens to be sensible guidance.

Sources indicate that there’s certainly a lot to learn from Italian grandmothers. Italy leads the European Union in life expectancy, and it’s a country where the number of centenarians is growing. A cluster of villages in Sardinia is one of the world’s five Blue Zones. Online guidance includes ditching social media, eating homemade everything, wearing cotton nightgowns, and welcoming unhurried lunches with friends. Some of these suggestions line up with how I’ve seen Italian grandmas live. But as a health and science journalist, I’ve noticed there’s more to it than what looks good on Instagram or TikTok. In fact, Licia Fertz, a 96-year-old Italian nonna based in Viterbo, Italy, tells SELF, quite the opposite is true.

“I put on my makeup and dress in cheerful colors, even if I’m not leaving the house, because presenting yourself well is an act of self-love,” Fertz says.

It seems that Italian nonne are the health gurus we all need. Read on to learn their secrets to a happier, healthier, and longer life.

I rarely see Italian nonne who don’t look their age. In fact, it’s one of the first things I noticed when I moved here. At the pools and beaches, it doesn’t matter how old they are; women, nonne included, frequently wear bikinis. Honestly, it’s refreshing and emphasizes a cultural mindset that aging is a natural part of life.

In a recent development, fertz tells SELF that this mindset is key to her living a long and healthy life. “Never think of yourself as old,” notes Fertz. “You are born young.”.

It turns out that as you age, having a more positive attitude about getting older could help you live longer too. A recent study found an association between how women view aging and the actual pace at which they age.

Sonja Lyubomirsky, a distinguished professor of psychology at the University of California, Riverside, and author of How To Feel Loved, tells SELF that a mindset is like putting on a pair of glasses or a coat. “It certainly matters very much what our mindset is when we think about aging,” Lyubomirsky states. “Is it a gift? Is it about wisdom, maturity, and the richness of life, or is it about deterioration and loss?” Both can be true, she says. “But you can choose.”.

At school pick-up for my daughter, I don’t only see other parents. I also see Italian nonne. That’s because Italian grandmas are very involved in their grandkids’ lives and take an active role in caregiving. In fact, for better or worse, the Italian economy is supported by the unpaid labor of Italian grandmothers—and this is well-known and discussed in local mom groups.

Sources indicate that research indicates that caregiving later in life may lead to better aging and act as a buffer against cognitive decline. One recent study found that grandparents who provided childcare—ranging from caring for sick grandkids, helping with homework, or driving them to school—scored higher on memory and verbal fluency tests compared with those who didn’t help with childcare.

In a recent development, “I live with my grandson,” Fertz tells SELF. “I’m a great-grandmother, and every day spent with my great-granddaughter is a gift that never ceases to amaze me.”.

Even if you’re not a grandparent, helping others can yield similar health benefits. According to research published in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine, people who volunteered more than 100 hours a year—versus those who volunteered zero hours a year—had a reduced risk of mortality, more optimism, and purpose in their lives.

It has been revealed that italian cities and villages are highly walkable, meaning walking isn’t something people do for exercise; it’s just a way of life. Even if someone has a car, sometimes a destination is only reachable by foot because Italy’s infamously narrow streets. Gas is also more expensive in Italy. While this might be inconvenient for some, a walking-first lifestyle happens to be associated with longevity.

“Walking is the most fundamental form of human physical activity and many, many hundreds of studies confirm that walking helps people age slower and better,” Daniel Lieberman, a professor of Human Evolutionary Biology at Harvard University, tells SELF. “Walking helps you age well.”.

Paola Mariotti, a pediatrician and nonna based in Florence, Italy, tells SELF that walking is very vital to her, and was very important to her own grandparents, who didn’t have a car and walked everywhere. Today, as a more modern nonna, Mariotti focuses on walking at least 5,000 steps a day—which she tracks on her phone—but strives to get 10,000 steps or more, if possible, each day.

Much of America isn’t walkable, but a 2025 study published in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine found that even 15 minutes of fast walking a day can reduce premature death.

At cafés in Italy, I’m always struck by how Italian nonne drink un caffè. Usually, she is just enjoying her coffee and watching people walk by, rather than scrolling on her phone or sending emails on her laptop. Some might call this the dolce far niente, which means the sweetness of doing nothing. While it’s true that these moments of pause and presence are more common in Italy, there’s something deeper to them. They reflect how, as a culture, Italians are content to live more mindfully. They appreciate quality over quantity and don’t feel the need to constantly multitask for the sake of being productive.

In fact, Jonathan Alpert, a psychotherapist in Upcoming York, tells SELF that he thinks nonnamaxxing has less to do with actual Italian grandmothers and more about Gen Z’s desire to escape hustle culture. “The appeal here is the fantasy of a life that feels grounded, warm, and unhurried,” Alpert notes. “A lot of younger people are burned out by the pressure to constantly optimize themselves, be productive, and turn their lives into content.”.

While in the moment, multitasking can feel like you’re being more efficient, researchers say that it actually does the opposite and can lead to increased stress levels.

In a recent development, the antidote to hustle culture is a mindful one. This can be as simple as just enjoying a coffee without much else, as it’s been found that people who stay in the present moment age better and with more resilience.

Sources indicate that in Italy, there’s an emphasis on eating what’s in season. In fact, my local market provides customers with a chart that identifies exactly what fruits and vegetables are in season each month. This lifestyle isn’t exactly optional—produce that’s out-of-season is harder to come by. Antonino De Lorenzo, professor emeritus of human nutrition at the University of Rome Tor Vergata, tells SELF that the value isn’t in the variety of food, but in what’s gained when you choose seasonal produce, which is food that is less likely to have preservatives and industrial products.

Recent findings suggest that “Freshness, variety, ripeness, and preparation methods can all exert a significant influence on a food’s nutritional profile,” De Lorenzo indicates. “A high-quality diet, maintained over time, promotes healthier aging, characterized by better preservation of physical, mental, and cognitive functions, as well as reduced exposure to major chronic diseases.”.

It has been revealed that indeed, the Mediterranean diet, which focuses on olive oil, vegetables, fruits, whole grains and legumes—all popular in Italy—has been linked to longevity. As researchers tend to emphasize, the Mediterranean diet isn’t a fad diet. It’s a way of life.

Italian grandmas are stereotypically known for being connected to their communities and neighbors—maybe even a bit too much, in the sense that it can veer into nosiness. Viral videos on social media have joked that Italian nonne are Italy’s security systems.

According to recent reports, “The most important thing for living a long and happy life? Don’t isolate yourself,” Fertz indicates. “Always stay in touch with people, travel, initiative outings, and get out of the house.”.

According to a study in The American Journal of Geriatric Psychiatry, having a sense of purpose can help preserve cognitive function as you age. A separate study found that people with a higher sense of purpose had a reduced risk for depression and loneliness. Whether that is being in-the-know in your community, or finding a hobby to keep you busy, the key is to feel connected and busy.

Because boredom, Fertz notes, is “the one thing that truly makes you old.”.

Why has North Korea redesigned its flag? It's not about aesthetics...

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (655 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Creativebloq

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, despite being a failed nation in most regards (60% are thought to be below the poverty line, and reports of widespread starvation have surfaced as recently as 2021), North Korea continues to fascinate us.
  • As the summit wrapped up today, though, Kim Jong Un was nowhere to be seen.
  • Well, earlier this month it emerged that the highly secretive and repressive nation has changed the shape of its flag for the first time since 1948.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, despite being a failed nation in most regards (60% are thought to be below the poverty line, and reports of widespread starvation have surfaced as recently as 2021), North Korea continues to fascinate us. Even this week, as Trump, Putin and Xi prepared to meet in Shenzhen, China the media was playing "Where's Kim?" after Trump told reporters North Korean leader Kim Jong Un "would like to" attend, and that whether he came was "up to President Xi".

As the summit wrapped up today, though, Kim Jong Un was nowhere to be seen. Instead, state media highlighted him touring a half-built ski resort at home. Which is shame for a design obsessive like me. Because if he had turned up, I'd have been watching the flagpoles rather than the handshakes.

Why? Well, earlier this month it emerged that the highly secretive and repressive nation has changed the shape of its flag for the first time since 1948.

The revised constitution, ratified in March but only recently published on the state website, sets the ratio at 1:1.65 rather than the old 1:2. The white stripes look noticeably thicker, and the red star in its white circle now sits closer to the centre. The government, though hasn't explained why, so it's up to us to have an educated guess.

Sources indicate that it's tempting to read this in pure design terms, as a long overdue tidy-up. Indeed, as long ago as 1948, one delegate worried the long, thin flag would fold too easily on the pole. And things do move slowly in state bureaucracies, after all. Not usually this slowly, but could it just be that sorting out the flag's ratio has finally just floated to the top of a long list of priorities?

Industry observers note that if it were as simple as that, though, North Korea would presumably have gone for the standard ratio of 2:3, the one seen in over 80 national flags. France, Spain, Italy, Netherlands, China, Russia, Ukraine… you get the picture. Instead Pyongyang has opted for on 1:1.65, a ratio seen in… absolutely no other national flag on Earth. Which kind of suggests they're trying to make a point.

According to recent reports, the professed meaning behind the design has shifted too. The white elements once stood for the purity of a single Korean people. Naenara now says they represent the loyalty of people who support the Party and the leader.

You might think "so what?", but this actually a very substantial deal. Ever since North and South Korea were split between the communist and capitalist powers in 1945, both sides have dreamed the unification of the country (albeit under their control, of course).

In 2023, though, Kim expounded the "two hostile states" doctrine, which stated that reunification “can never be achieved” with South Korea. In 2024 he rewrote the national anthem along these lines, and the latest flag design should be seen in the same light.

It's a bit like when you give up on getting back with an ex-partner: you go out and buy a whole upcoming outfit to cheer yourself up and show them you're doing just fine without them.

According to recent reports, so while the flag design that has barely changed, that's doesn't mean it's not significant. The fact that it's changed at all actually says a lot about the future of 70 million Koreans, and the global world order as a whole.

Tech Report: How to pick the right website template for your creative business

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1259 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Creativebloq

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Even if you're using one of the best website builders, I recommend taking your time when choosing your template if you're going that route.
  • Sources indicate that templates can still offer substantial value by handling the heavy lifting of page structure, navigation, and responsive design.
  • In this guide, we'll cover the key factors to consider when evaluating templates, and also what other options are available if a template-based approach isn't the best match for your project.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Even if you're using one of the best website builders, I recommend taking your time when choosing your template if you're going that route. A website template provides the foundation for everything, and choosing wisely at the beginning can save you time and energy further down the line.

Sources indicate that templates can still offer substantial value by handling the heavy lifting of page structure, navigation, and responsive design. But with countless websites vying for attention, you'll want a starting point that aligns with your brand while leaving plenty of scope for customisation so you can make the site stand out and add features or adapt the site later without requiring a complete overhaul.

In this guide, we'll cover the key factors to consider when evaluating templates, and also what other options are available if a template-based approach isn't the best match for your project.

Modern templates aren't intended to be finished websites but to provide a flexible framework that can be reshaped to fit your needs. That said, it's still important to check that a template includes all the layout and navigation features you think you're going to need. Success comes down to choosing a template that's already close to your brand's requirements, then refining and personalising it until the final result feels unique and tailored rather than generic.

In a recent development, pay close attention to the underlying framework, including page layout, content hierarchy and overall site structure. Modern website builders make it relatively simple to enhancement colors, typography, images and other visual details, but altering navigation systems, restructuring pages, or reworking the flow of content can be far more time-consuming, so these are areas to check.

Make sure the template offers the sections or content blocks that you need. This might include a hero image, features, testimonials and galleries. You might only want a simple one pager, but remember that it's easier to simplify a complex template than it is to add structure to one that's overly basic. Templates that provide little flexibility could limit future content growth.

Check the menu organisation fits with the structure you want before committing. Look for a clear visual hierarchy that guides visitors to notable content, intuitive menus that make sections easy to find, flexible page layouts that support your content requirements and logical placements for calls to action, such as contact forms or portfolio links.

Avoid choosing a template based solely on appearance without considering usability or selecting complex navigation structures that confuse visitors. Overcrowded layouts can confuse viewers with elements that compete for attention.

The visual style of a template should complement your brand rather than dominate it, and design elements should align with your brand identity and audience expectations.

Most modern templates will allow considerable customisation, so you don't necessarily need one that resembles your branding from the start, but it can save time. Even then, publishing a template without significant customisation is rarely enough so check that typography and spacing can be easily adapted and that the colour palette can be customised. Also check that visual styling is consistent throughout the template.

Recent findings suggest that web design trends come and go. In 2026, we're seeing a lot of glassmorphism, immersive 3D visuals and storytelling through motion. But avoid picking a trendy design that may date rapidly. Using a template with excessive animations or visual effects can also cause a site to date, while also potentially impacting on loading times and user engagement.

According to recent reports, with visitors browsing on desktops, tablets and smartphones, responsive design is essential. Check how the template adapts across devices, as restructuring mobile layouts requires advanced customisation.

That means more than just checking that the layout adapts to the different screen size and orientation. Also evaluate whether animations, transitions, and interactive components work across platforms and match your brand's personality.

While most templates today are responsive, don't assume completely responsive behaviour without testing it. Look for layouts that adapt smoothly to different screen sizes, readable text and appropriately sized buttons on mobile devices and fast-loading pages across platforms. Functionality should ideally be consistent regardless of device.

It has been revealed that prioritising responsiveness can also mean avoiding designs that rely heavily on large images or complex interactions. Make sure you remember to check how portfolios, galleries or forms display on smaller screens.

According to recent reports, most websites need to connect with external tools and services. Your template should support these integrations without unnecessary complications, so ensure the template is compatible with features like ecommerce tools, booking systems, or membership areas even if you're only considering adding these at a later stage. It could set you back a lot if you decide to add a store in the future and find that the template doesn't readily support it.

Look for compatibility with your preferred content management system (many people use WordPress), and support for e-commerce, booking systems or payment gateways if required. You might also want easy integration with analytics, marketing and social media tools, regular updates and compatibility with third-party plugins.

In a recent development, avoid assuming that all integrations will work out of the box. At the same time, don't overcomplicate the site with unnecessary third-party features that you don't think you'll really need.

In a recent development, using a template can still be an efficient way to get online, but advances in AI mean that there are now alternatives that exist, still without having to code anything from scratch. AI website builders have become sophisticated enough to serve as legitimate starting points, with platforms like Bluehost creating custom designs based on conversational inputs.

The Bluehost AI Website Builder can turn a simple business description into a complete, working WordPress website in minutes. The platform guides you through a few basic questions about your business, or you can simply enter a prompt about your goals and brand style.

The AI builds a full layout that's automatically populated with pre-written text, navigation so you can get a good sense of how the site will look. You can then interact conversationally with an AI assistant to rewrite the copy, adjust tone, add pages or replace images.

Recent findings suggest that you can also get more granular and fine-tune text, images and layouts using a visual drag-and-drop editor like you would with a template. And unlike closed website builders, the builder runs on WordPress. You keep full content ownership, and you can access the WordPress dashboard, install plugins, or use WooCommerce for online stores.

In a recent development, paid prepares bundle reliable hosting, free SSL security, a Content Delivery Network (CDN), weekly automated backups, malware scanning, and a free custom domain for the first year. You can also take advantage of tools like Yoast SEO Premium access to help optimise page titles, meta descriptions and readability.

#45754. 6 Supplements Doctors Actually Take

📅 10 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1502 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Self ↗ Open Full Page

6 Supplements Doctors Actually Take

📅 10 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1502 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • These days, it seems like everyone is taking a supplement—to look better, think better, sleep better, relax better, poop better, or work out better.
  • Sources indicate that supplements may be ubiquitous, but many experts have serious reservations about their rise.
  • Still, there are exceptions to every rule—and supplements are no different.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

These days, it seems like everyone is taking a supplement—to look better, think better, sleep better, relax better, poop better, or work out better. And you’re not imagining things: Half of adults and one-third of children in the United States take supplements regularly, according to the Office of Dietary Supplements.

Sources indicate that supplements may be ubiquitous, but many experts have serious reservations about their rise. First, most physicians recommend obtaining nutrients directly from food rather than a pill or capsule. Second, supplements aren’t reviewed for safety and effectiveness by the FDA before they hit shelves. Because of all the concerns surrounding supplements, Jeffrey Linder, MD, MPH, a general internist and professor of medicine at the Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine, takes a dim view of the category overall: In fact, “a vast majority of supplements are probably worthless,” he tells SELF.

Still, there are exceptions to every rule—and supplements are no different. Many experts, as it turns out, do take some type of supplement, but they are choosy about which ones they select. Read on to learn more about six they actually use.

Industry observers note that how it works: Vitamin D plays key roles in bone health and immune function. In fact, low vitamin D is associated with a wide swath of medical conditions, according to Dr. Linder—including cancer, autoimmune diseases, infectious diseases, and cardiovascular problems (and, famously, seasonal affective disorder, or SAD).

Why some docs like it: Vitamin D deficiency is widespread, especially among people who live at northern latitudes that don’t see as much sun during the winter, and people with darker skin. What’s more, few foods contain significant amounts of vitamin D, so it’s tough to source enough from your diet. Lawrence Green, MD, a dermatologist and clinical professor at the George Washington University School of Medicine and Health Sciences, tells SELF that these two factors make vitamin D a rare nutrient “we do need to take supplements for.” Nearly every single one of the eight doctors who spoke with SELF for this article noted they take a vitamin D supplement, especially in the winter, though the frequency and dosage varied.

What to keep in mind: Most docs recommend vitamin D3 (also known as cholecalciferol) over vitamin D2 (also known as ergocalciferol), as studies have shown that D3 is more effective at raising vitamin D levels in your blood. Whichever option you decide on, try to take it with food—specifically, an item that contains fat. Because vitamin D is a fat-soluble nutrient, it “absorbs better that way,” Sara Velayati, MD, an obesity medicine specialist at Montefiore Einstein and an assistant professor at Albert Einstein College of Medicine in Upcoming York City, tells SELF. For this reason, Dr. Green makes a point of taking his supplements with breakfast or dinner. “The fattier and thicker the meal,” the better, he indicates.

According to recent reports, what it does: Calcium is a mineral that helps build and maintain strong bones and teeth. Women in their 40s approaching menopausal age should make it a particular priority to ensure their intake is adequate, Rachel Pessah-Pollack, MD, an endocrinologist at NYU Langone Health and a clinical professor at the NYU Grossman School of Medicine, tells SELF, as the physical changes that come with perimenopause and menopause can heighten bone loss and downstream health conditions like osteoporosis.

Industry observers note that who takes it: Like the other supplements on this list, calcium is best sourced from your diet, Dr. Pessah-Pollack says. “But if you’re not able to (I try to get dairy products but often come up short), a supplement is needed.” She takes a combined calcium and vitamin D tablet daily, as vitamin D helps calcium absorb.

How to take it: “The type of calcium supplements you are taking matters,” Dr. Pessah-Pollack claims. Calcium carbonate and calcium citrate are the two most common. “Calcium carbonate should be taken with food because it requires gastric acid to be absorbed,” Dr. Pessah-Pollack says. Calcium citrate is an alternative that can be taken with or without food.

Sources indicate that how it works: Magnesium is a mineral that can enhance sleep and muscle recovery. Research has also shown that it’s effective at preventing migraines, Raquel Zemtsov, MD, MPH, a family medicine doctor and assistant professor at the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine, tells SELF.

Why some docs like it: In addition to Dr. Zemtsov, who takes magnesium to stave off migraine symptoms, Dr. Velayati takes magnesium for the sleep benefits. Likewise, Sheeva Talebian, MD, a reproductive endocrinologist at CCRM Fertility of Newly introduced York, and Kathleen Jordan, MD, an internal medicine physician and chief medical officer at Midi Health, also turn to it at bedtime to boost their shut-eye.

What to keep in mind: Some types of magnesium are better tolerated, claims Dr. Velayati—something to note if you’re especially sensitive to side effects. Magnesium glycinate “avoids the gastrointestinal upset caused by magnesium oxides and magnesium citrates,” for example, Dr. Jordan says. Depending on your needs, however, magnesium glycinate might not be the best option: Magnesium oxide is the recommended magnesium type for migraines, so that’s the one Dr. Zemtsov keeps on hand, for example. Taking magnesium with food can also help prevent GI distress, according to Dr. Velayati.

It has been revealed that how it works: Omega-3 fatty acids are polyunsaturated fats that are notable for cardiovascular health. Common omega-3 supplements include fish oil and krill oil.

Recent findings suggest that why some docs like it: Dr. Jordan, Dr. Talebian, and Dr. Velayati all take omega-3s. “With their anti-inflammatory properties and association with improved brain health, this is a popular supplement among physicians, myself included,” Dr. Jordan, who takes krill oil, says. Similarly, Dr. Velayati dabbles in fish oil, but takes it selectively. “The right dose really depends on the goal, but I don’t think it’s necessary for everyone,” she says.

What to keep in mind: Fish oil supplements can have a characteristic fishy aftertaste, so it might take some trial and error to find one that works for you (read: doesn’t leave you gagging). What’s more, absorption and bioavailability can be a challenge, according to Dr. Jordan. Because omega-3s, like vitamin D, are fat-soluble, taking fish oil with a meal that contains fat can help skirt this problem. Some claim krill oil doesn’t cause the dreaded aftertaste as much as fish oil, and evidence suggests it’s also better absorbed by the body.

According to recent reports, how it works: Iron, a mineral, acts as an essential ingredient in hemoglobin, a protein found in your red blood cells. Without enough iron, your blood won’t be able to carry out its core task of delivering oxygen to organs and tissues, resulting in anemia.

Sources indicate that why some docs like it: Iron deficiency is common in women due to the loss of blood during menstruation every month. “Occasionally, despite trying my hardest to seek out iron-rich foods, I still develop an iron deficiency,” Dr. Zemtsov states. When that happens, she takes ferrous gluconate (a particular type of iron supplement) every other day to treat or prevent anemia, since research indicates iron supplements are better absorbed and cause fewer side effects that way. Dr. Jordan also takes iron supplements, citing the advantages for sleep, hair health, and overall energy.

Industry observers note that what to keep in mind: Iron absorption is enhanced by vitamin C, so pairing your iron supplement with a food that contains vitamin C or even a vitamin C supplement—as Dr. Zemtsov does—can be helpful.

In a recent development, how it works: Fiber, a type of carb, boosts digestion in a variety of ways: It keeps you full, helps prevent constipation, and supports bowel health. Besides the GI stuff, it also serves other functions in your body, including stabilizing your blood sugar and lowering “bad” LDL cholesterol.

According to recent reports, why some docs like it: “Unless you are that rare woman who regularly gets in her 25 to 30 grams per day, extra fiber intake is beneficial for almost everyone, and addresses multiple challenges for me personally, including prediabetes and a rising cholesterol level,” Dr. Jordan says. She takes a fiber supplement as needed, on days when she doesn’t manage to hit her goal.

What to keep in mind: If your body isn’t acclimated to a high fiber intake, suddenly bombarding it could cause some digestive distress (think gas and bloating), so start slow to ease the transition. You’ll also need to increase your water intake simultaneously, since fiber requires water to work.

Sources indicate that “When someone is considering a supplement, I usually recommend having a specific reason for taking it”—like a confirmed nutritional deficiency, Dr. Velayati says. “Overall, I view supplements as a way to fill a gap, not a substitute for good nutrition, sleep, exercise, and evidence-based medical care.” The bottom line: Supplements are really meant for plugging holes in your diet.

Photography by Rory Gaylor.

London studio ConForm Architects has transformed a former cattle barn into a multifunctional space for a working farm in the Cotswolds, contrasting its original red-brick and timber structure with zinc and black-timber additions.

Named Open Byre, the 124-square-metre barn has been adapted into a flexible space for meetings and gatherings, with the first floor containing a standalone apartment for guests.

ConForm Architects‘ design responds to the dual nature of the barn’s surroundings – with traditional red-brick farm structures to the east and more contemporary agricultural barns to the east – combining restoration with a fresh contrasting palette of stone, metal and timber.

In a recent development, “The design centres on a dialogue between old and newly introduced. Rather than blending the interventions into the existing fabric, we wanted each to remain legible and reinforce the other,” studio partner Ben Edgley told Dezeen.

“The building sits between two distinct parts of the farm: the older red brick buildings around the formal front farmyard and the more recent, industrial agricultural structures beyond,” he added.

“The design responds to both, retaining the brickwork and slate roof at the front while using zinc and blackened timber at the rear to reference the newer farm buildings.”.

A defining feature of the barn’s fresh rear facade is a projecting volume wrapped by gabion walls, filled with locally-quarried stone and punctured by a large window illuminating a cross-laminated timber (CLT) staircase.

In the ground floor’s flexible office and arts spaces, the idea of material contrasts continues, with original red-brick walls and repaired timber ceilings accompanied by joinery including desks, storage and a bathroom pod in black through-coloured MDF.

Above, the guest apartment is tucked beneath the exposed beams of the barn’s roof, with its own dedicated living room, kitchen-diner and bathroom finished in matching black timber.

“The central CLT stair is the defining gesture. It brings together structure, circulation and spatial organisation, drawing the eye from the entrance through the building towards the trees beyond,” noted Edgley.

“Its scale and material presence establish a clear contrast with the existing brickwork and timber frame,” he added.

Sources indicate that “The clients were closely involved in the process, undertaking much of the timber repair alongside local craftsmen. Their commitment to retaining the original fabric was central to the project.”.

ConForm Architects was founded in 2017 by Edgley alongside Eoin O’Leary.

Previous projects by the studio include a terraced home in London with perforated metal floors to filter daylight and a green-terrazzo flat extension modelled on bay windows.

Photography by Rory Gaylor.

GTA 6’s NPCs are built to the same visual standard as Jason and Lucia

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that every open-world game has a crowd problem.
  • Having spent time in Leonida myself for my GTA 6 review, often just people-watching, eavesdropping on conversations, and spying on the game's background actors as they play out their lives, I can say this is the most alive game I've played.
  • With all I've seen, I can see why Rockstar's art team is so keen to talk about its pedestrians and background characters.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that every open-world game has a crowd problem. Pack the streets with people and, sooner or later, you clock the same jogger for the fifth time, and the illusion falls apart. GTA 6 breaks that wall and delivers a world filled with unique little virtual actors.

Having spent time in Leonida myself for my GTA 6 review, often just people-watching, eavesdropping on conversations, and spying on the game's background actors as they play out their lives, I can say this is the most alive game I've played. A regular couple rant about gentrification and other conspiracies on their apartment steps; two others argue about that latest Manatees result; two women sip coffee, gossiping about their friend's love life; one's eyes widen, brows lift, just a fraction too slowly to feel like shock.

With all I've seen, I can see why Rockstar's art team is so keen to talk about its pedestrians and background characters.

In a recent development, valmor Garcia, Senior Technical Art Director: Dynamic Art, indicates Rockstar has moved on from the “monolithic” NPCs of GTAV and Red Dead Redemption 2, which were built to lower visual standards than those of the games’ main casts. The aim now is “fully fleshed-out characters with singular awareness and visual identities”, driven by dynamic moods and personalities, with their own anatomy, facial features and dialogue.

In a recent development, garcia puts all of that on a visual par with Jason and Lucia. He also notes it’s the first time Rockstar feels it has levelled the whole cast so consistently, including world NPCs.

In a recent development, valmor Garcia, Senior Technical Art Director: Dynamic Art, says Rockstar has moved on from the “monolithic” NPCs of GTAV and Red Dead Redemption 2, which were built to lower visual standards than those of the games’ main casts. The aim now is “fully fleshed-out characters with singular awareness and visual identities”, driven by dynamic moods and personalities, with their own anatomy, facial features and dialogue.

Garcia puts all of that on a visual par with Jason and Lucia. He also notes it’s the first time Rockstar feels it has levelled the whole cast so consistently, including world NPCs.

It has been revealed that mark Tennant, Vice President of Animation, conveys the scale. “There are close to a thousand animation sets for ambient activities,” he says, “then we layer in hundreds of bespoke one-off events and custom sequences to punctuate the world and reward exploration.”.

In a recent development, those everyday sets, with people hanging out and doing day-to-day jobs, “form the foundation of this living world”, according to Tennant. The variety extends to bodies, too. The team decided early to “really push the variation in character sizes and body types”, which meant building “a very robust way to share animations between characters”.

Recent findings suggest that garcia says the team built new technology and tools “from the ground up” for the engine. The all-new in-house tech covers hair, cloth simulation and head-and-body customisation, and it’s applied across the world “to benefit all characters equally”. So the people on the street get the same tech as the leads.

Sources indicate that it’s the little things that sell it. John Macpherson, Senior Design Director: World & Population, says that “everywhere you look, little stories constantly unfold”. That might be as simple as what someone’s wearing, how they walk and talk, or what they’re blasting from a passing car.

Recent findings suggest that I see this in how characters dress and behave differently across the map. Some things are just obvious, such as characters wearing swimsuits on the beach, but Rockstar takes it further, as Leonida's beachgoers lie and chat on towels, play frisbee, and make mistakes – I snuck onto a boat party and watched as characters danced and reacted to Lucia and Jason's moves.

In a recent development, most of the people you pass in Leonida will only be on screen for a moment, but Rockstar has built them as if you might stop and look; in fact, the developer wants you to stop, look and listen, and simply love being in the world. Sam Fender's People Watching is on the soundtrack for a reason.

#45749. Are Single Older Ladies Really Happy Without Marriage? Experts Weigh In

📅 13 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1510 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Self ↗ Open Full Page

Are Single Older Ladies Really Happy Without Marriage? Experts Weigh In

📅 13 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1510 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • At some point in most women’s lives, a familiar line of thinking creeps in—whether on its own or planted by well-meaning parents: What if I don’t get married?
  • According to recent reports, for Joan, the panic hit in her 30s—strong enough to land her in a psychologist’s office.
  • Someone deeply absorbed in his own life—his job, his hobbies, his community.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At some point in most women’s lives, a familiar line of thinking creeps in—whether on its own or planted by well-meaning parents: What if I don’t get married? What if I never find my person and end up alone?

According to recent reports, for Joan, the panic hit in her 30s—strong enough to land her in a psychologist’s office. Back then, she indicates, “a woman who didn’t want a husband was assumed to have something wrong with her.” But her therapist—married with children, yet more open-minded than most—didn’t try to correct her with cheesy motivational mantras or fear tactics about a “ticking clock.” Instead, she asked a different question: What kind of husband would you want, if you had one?

Joan listed a few traits. Someone busy, she recalls saying. Someone deeply absorbed in his own life—his job, his hobbies, his community.

“So you'd want someone intellectually stimulating?” her therapist asked.

In a recent development, “No,” Joan replied. “I’d want someone who’s never home.”.

It landed as a joke, though deep down, it wasn’t. What came from that session was an almost accidental realization that sounded radical at the time (it was around 1980): “Some people genuinely live their best lives independently,” Joan tells me. Now 79, single, and uninterested in changing her relationship status, she has spent decades proving her theory true.

Industry observers note that for much of modern history, women like Joan were cast as anomalies, freaks, or worse: cautionary tales. There’s “the childless cat lady.” The “old maid.” The “lonely spinster.” Singlehood was framed as a transitional phase, a temporary stop on the way to finding the One. Not an end goal, and certainly not a fulfilling one.

But the stigma is softening—and the older, unmarried women of this generation are living proof that a life without a husband isn’t a fallback; it’s a deeply satisfying choice.

Sources indicate that you can see it in the collective fatigue around modern dating (78% of consumers on apps including Tinder, Hinge, and Bumble reported feeling burnt out, per a recent Forbes Health survey). Young adults in their mid 20s to early 30s (the supposed “prime marriage years”) are having far less sex than previous generations, with sexual inactivity up roughly 50% for women over the past decade. The shift reveals up in pop culture too—in particular, the growing appetite for plots that sideline romance in favor of friendship, independence, and chosen families (like in Barbie and Wicked).

It has been revealed that but perhaps the clearest proof is in lived experiences. The several 70-somethings I spoke with for this story have been single for decades—and aren’t wishing they’d done it any differently. If anything, their lives carry a sense of ease and expansiveness. Many describe weekly, laughter-filled girls’ nights and happy hours; solo trips planned on a whim; financial freedom to buy property, adopt pets, start small businesses…literally do whatever they want, whenever they want. A few still date casually, dipping in and out of steamy flings only when it suits them. Others have opted out of romance entirely. “My favorite part?” one 73-year-old woman tells me bluntly. “Not having to bicker or put up with an incompetent man. That’s probably why I’m the least stressed I’ve ever been.”.

Across their stories, there’s no regret or hint of “missing out.” Just single older ladies enjoying where they are—nothing like the caricatures of the bitter man-hater or the desperate, unlucky romantic we’re used to seeing.

In a recent development, as Joan is quick to point out, “not everyone starts off wanting a romantic relationship and then moves on to singlehood as Plan B.” It’s a perspective that’s become increasingly common, so much so that sociologist Bella DePaulo, PhD, built a framework (and wrote a book) about it: being Single at Heart. These are women (including herself) who don’t end up alone; they orient toward it as a genuine preference.

In a recent development, “I still smile when I think about the men I dated when I was a very young adult,” Dr. DePaulo, 72, tells me. “But I remember even more fondly how I felt when each of those relationships ended: finally free.”.

The practical benefits of singledom—solitude, strong friendships, fewer relational stressors—aren’t exclusive to unmarried folks. “But in my opinion, couples are never free the way single people are,” Dr. DePaulo claims. The difference, she claims, is psychological: the ability to structure a day, a life, or a passing thought without reflexively factoring in another person’s needs or reactions. “A romantic partner is also there in your mind almost all the time,” Dr. DePaulo points out—even if only on the periphery. “That might be comforting for some. But it can also feel a bit unwelcome, as if they’re always considering what their significant other may be wanting or feeling.” Remove that, and your attention and energy become fully your own.

According to recent reports, of course, the ability to choose this lifestyle is relatively recent. For centuries, marriage wasn’t just a matter of romance—women relied on it for financial stability, social acceptance, and a sanctioned path to family, Kris Marsh, PhD, sociologist and author of The Love Jones Cohort: Single and Living Alone in the Black Middle Class, tells SELF. But with greater access to education, careers, and economic independence (along with broader definitions of intimacy, family, and fulfillment), the pressure to couple up has eased. As of 2023, 42% of US adults were unpartnered, according to the Pew Research Center (up from 29% in 1990). And among the non-daters younger than 50, half aren’t interested in a relationship—though enjoying your single status doesn’t have to involve an anti-love attitude.

Industry observers note that “Now, a lot of women are looking for something additive,” Dr. Marsh says. “I’ve heard over and over, ‘I’m already in a very good place on my own. So you can’t be a distraction. You can’t disrupt my peace.’” Though for most, that epiphany doesn’t happen overnight.

Alice Foster, who recently turned 80, is a classic example of someone who followed the cultural script handed to many in her generation: marry young, raise children, enjoy the stability. “It was fine, but I felt like it was never really about me,” Foster tells SELF. “It wasn’t my life.”.

Industry observers note that in 1988, her marriage ended in divorce—though what followed wasn’t the loss she had been taught to fear. It was space. Peace. Recalibration. She moved upstate. Went back to school. Built a fresh career in nursing. Slowly, she began constructing a life that finally felt like her own.

“I feel like I’m in my 50s. It’s been so fun,” she reflects. “I love being retired. I love traveling. I love having people visit me. I love not having to answer to anybody. I’ve been single for so long and loving this life so much that, honestly, I don’t want to get tied down.” And that, experts say, is often how it works.

According to recent reports, rather than being a fixed moral stance or a lifelong rejection of romance, singlehood tends to be a lived, flexible experience—an acceptance of being on your own that you don’t always realize you’re choosing until later. Maybe, like Foster, you leave an unsatisfying marriage. You pull back on exhaustive online dating. You decide this is the year you’ll focus on work, hobbies, or travel. Over time, you stop planning life around the possibility of a relationship…and start seeing that you already have the joy you thought only a husband could provide.

Still, a question tends to linger: Are these women actually happy?

In a recent development, recent research suggests yes—in fact, satisfaction with singlehood tends to increase with age, starting for people in their 40s. Despite cultural progress, there’s still skepticism as to why anyone would willingly stay single. Whereas married people are taken at their word when they claim fulfillment (even though we know that’s not always true), those who deviate face public scrutiny. “They have to be extra strong, exceptionally confident to stand comfortably in their singleness and validate to the world that they are, in fact, thriving,” Dr. Marsh adds—an expectation that flattens single older ladies into either a hyper-independent success story or a pitiable failure, with little room for nuance.

Sources indicate that but that pressure can have an unintended effect too. After decades of being asked by society to justify their lifestyle, many simply stop performing. All of the women I spoke with didn’t overexplain. They weren’t defensive. They didn’t seem especially interested in winning me over.

Recent findings suggest that it takes a certain kind of confidence and clarity to stop shaping your life around what’s expected and historically rewarded, and instead follow what feels good, without apology. What you get then, as Dr. Marsh has observed in her research, is a quieter, rarer form of happiness—one that isn’t performed and doesn’t ask for external validation. Instead, it feels much more genuine. It endures.

#45747. This beautiful logo design was created to grow like nature

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Creativebloq ↗ Open Full Page

This beautiful logo design was created to grow like nature

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (807 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Creativebloq

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, how do you rebrand a 200-year-old institution that wants its new logo to "feel like plants"?
  • And yet the latest identity for the Pennsylvania Horticultural Society achieves it.
  • In a recent development, turning 200 years old in 2027, the Pennsylvania Horticultural Society is only 50 years younger than the US as an independent country.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, how do you rebrand a 200-year-old institution that wants its new logo to "feel like plants"? Plants are constantly changing; they grow, wilt, bloom, move in the wind, shed their leaves and sprout new ones. Captivating that in a permanent identity built to last years might seem like an impossible task.

And yet the latest identity for the Pennsylvania Horticultural Society achieves it. The logo is a clear candidate as one of the best animated logos, and the blooming rebrand also includes one of the most beautiful brand manuals I've seen. There's even a flipbook, further demonstrating the dynamism of the mark.

In a recent development, turning 200 years old in 2027, the Pennsylvania Horticultural Society is only 50 years younger than the US as an independent country. To mark its upcoming anniversary, it brought in local design agency Smith & Diction to create an identity that better represents the breadth of what it does, from urban greening to landscaping parks and the City Harvest initiative.

According to recent reports, the existing logo design was fairly generic. It could have been the identity for a financial institution – or even a retirement home, as Smith & Diction point out. Depicting a single tree, it hardly represented the rich diversity of the plant kingdom. What kind of tree was it supposed to be anyway?

The agency's solution was a three-letter logo in which the letters become roots, with a different species of native plant growing from each. Smith & Diction says the process began with the illustrations. Summer McClure drew the plants and flowers within rectangles, chosen to represent Philadelphia's grid layout of city blocks.

Image credit: Pennsylvania Horticultural Society / Smith & Diction.

Image credit: Pennsylvania Horticultural Society / Smith & Diction.

Industry observers note that the logo was then animated. Henrique Barone drew the plants growing from the letterforms, frame by frame. This allowed the creation of the flipbook (see the Instagram post below) as well as the final animation, which feels like a timelapse video from a nature documentary. A second animation was made by Justin Lawes to show the plants moving as if swaying in the breeze.

The result is a strong, versatile and dynamic logo that represents nature, the city grid, and the PHS's work to unite them.

A post shared by Smith & Diction — Design & Copywriting (@smith_diction).

It has been revealed that the logo's backed up by further custom brand illustrations based on native flora for social posts and things like menus and signs. There are also floral illustrations for sub brands, including a peony for the PHS's annual flower show.

The beauty of this system is that it introduces another way in which the branding can grow like a garden. The idea is that the PHS can host workshops where people will be able to draw their own florals to fit the same dimensions, or make their own linocut prints.

The colour palette is also unconventional, again reflecting the diversity of plant life. While there's a core set of greens and blues, the palette expands to contemplate dozens of colours. As for type, Caslon Doric is the lead, backed up by the elegance of ES Park, a choice inspired by the practical simplicity of old PHS exhibition posters.

Image credit: Pennsylvania Horticultural Society / Smith & Diction.

Image credit: Pennsylvania Horticultural Society / Smith & Diction.

According to recent reports, it's one of those projects that's blurs the line between brand design and art. That's apparent in the decision to produce a physical brand book, which was "designed as a reminder to touch grass and hold books".

In a recent development, "Making a shiny digital case study to talk about our partnership just felt inauthentic," Smith & Diction explains. "This isn’t a shiny digital brand, it’s rooted in the tangible: grass below your feet, warm sun on your face, the sound of birds chirping to one another from neighboring trees.".

You can purchase a copy of the book for $60 for which you also get the flip book, a lapel pin and a poster.

Joe is a regular freelance journalist and editor at Creative Bloq. A veteran news writer and photographer, he now works as a project manager at the London and Buenos Aires-based design, production and branding agency Hermana Creatives. There he manages a team of designers, photographers and video editors who specialise in producing visual content and design assets for the hospitality sector. He also dances Argentine tango.

The festival, which runs from 30 November to 6 December 2026, takes place across Miami, in neighbourhoods such as the Miami Design District and Miami Beach.

The event includes fairs, exhibitions, installations, open showrooms, talks, introduces, pop-up shops and parties throughout the week.

Highlights include the Design Miami and Art Basel Miami Beach fairs, alongside satellite fairs NADA Miami, Art Miami and Fridge Art Fair.

Alongside the guide, Dezeen has created an interactive map for the art week, helping attendees proposal their routes around the city.

There’s still time to feature in the Miami art week 2026 guide.

  • In a recent development, the significant draw of Unreal Engine 5 was speed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that when your physical set is three walls and a ceiling, whatever’s outside the window has to carry a lot of the film. For SNTIENT 2.0, the Fashion Innovation Agency’s film for London College of Fashion, that view was a bleak, abandoned city, and it lived entirely in Unreal Engine.

The story is a dystopia with a twist, set around the idea that resources have run out, humans have retreated into a simulation, and the robots left behind to look after the physical world have started to find beauty in it. “That gave us our visual starting point. A bleak, oppressive sci-fi environment with the potential for transformation,” says Dickon Knowles, director of content at Dandelion + Burdock. The finished film doesn't explore that transformation as far as originally planned, but the city still set the tone for everything else.

In a recent development, the significant draw of Unreal Engine 5 was speed. Working in a real-time engine meant the team could play with spaces, lighting, and textures, see the result straight away, and change it on the spot, instead of waiting for a render only to find it was wrong. “It made the whole process much more fluid,” Knowles notes.

Other routes were tried first. “We tried a couple of generative approaches to creating the city plate for the wall, but resolutions were an problem and the visual fidelity wasn’t there,” Knowles explains. “Which is why we reverted back to our existing Unreal Engine version.”.

Even then, the city needed work. The original environment was foggy and slightly desaturated, and wasn't reading through the camera as intended. Knowles reworked the fog, replacing the general wash through the scene with more detailed VDB fog, while reducing its overall presence and boosting the saturation, particularly in the city windows. The LED wall looked better with richer blacks and more contrast, which the fog had been fighting against. It needed a more vivid backdrop to work on camera.

Most of the city was already built before the shoot, with the team making visual refinements, grading and subtle tweaks on set. It wasn't building a digital world from scratch while the cameras were rolling. The advantage was seeing how those changes looked on the wall and through the camera, and making adjustments without waiting for a latest render.

The city also ran on an LED wall as the view from the character’s window, which gave the performer something real to react to rather than a green screen to imagine over.

Sources indicate that cinematographer Ben Saffer, whose company, Supervision VP, handled the virtual production, says the appeal was being able to capture everything together. The virtual and physical lighting could be controlled as one, so the glow on screen matched the light on set. “You’re doing it all in camera and capturing everything together at once, and you’re not having to guess at anything,” he says.

The alternatives were a green screen or a pre-rendered backdrop. Knowles says cost was less of a concern than visual quality, because the city content had already been created for a previous project. “The city lights reflect on the performer’s face and on the surfaces of the props and set,” he says. “There is a level of visual immersion that is hard to capture in a studio without the LED wall to illuminate the space.”.

The LED wall wasn't simply providing something pretty to look at outside the window; it was lighting the performer and the physical set at the same time, similar to how Magnopus used Unreal Engine for Fallout. The intention was to keep post-production to a minimum, getting the footage as close to the finished shot as possible during filming.

Unreal also solved a budget problem because the film needed a shutter that rises to reveal the city, but a moving shutter built into the set wasn't realistic on the budget, and adding one in VFX would have meant losing that in-camera moment.

It has been revealed that so the LED wall became the shutter, rising to reveal the digital city behind it. For reverse shots, a second wall on wheels could be brought in to act as a fourth wall. Because the content ran in real time, the team could quickly render upcoming assets for those angles, animate them, and get them moving. “It was nice to get that in camera,” Saffer notes.

Not everything went virtual, though, as the pod itself was a physical build, because the team wanted it to feel gritty and lived-in, with the LED wall and Unreal handling the distant environment. The AI-generated dream sequence at the start was a separate part of the production, created using generative tools to show the character floating in water before she wakes up.

It has been revealed that the film has very few beats: the character wakes, the window opens, she looks out. Saffer says the real challenge was getting a sense of the world and her place in it within two minutes. The team also had to make the most of the tiny space, shooting on an URSA Cine 17K 65 with prototype Atlas Lens Co. anamorphic lenses. The larger sensor meant Saffer could capture more of the set without resorting to an extreme wide-angle lens, which would have distorted the perspective.

It has been revealed that there was still room for a bit of old-fashioned experimentation. Towards the end of the film, as the character looks towards the window, Saffer held a plastic Polly Pocket toy in front of the lens and shone his phone torch through it from the side to create an optical effect. He also played around with cling film and other materials in front of the lens.
